https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/oli.text: The Budapest Times Oligarchs put on notice: pay up or face the consequences "We have already managed to recover assets worth thousands of billions for the Hungarian state and, with it, for the Hungarian people — and the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Agency is only just beginning its operations," Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote on his Facebook page on Tuesday. In a video uploaded alongside the post, the prime minister said that the asset recovery process he had committed to was proceeding step by step, already delivering concrete, visible results even before the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Agency had begun operating. On Monday, more than 100 billion forints in public funds were returned to the budget. He drew attention to the fact that Duna Aszfalt — linked to László Szíjj, an “oligarch” and business associate of Lőrinc Mészáros — announced, shortly after a complaint was filed by the Ministry of Economy and Energy, that it would repay 400 million dollars, equivalent to more than 100 billion forints, to state-owned banks. According to him, Duna Aszfalt had been one of the biggest winners of public procurement over the past decade and a half; the company won more than 600 billion forints’ worth of public procurement contracts between 2018 and 2020, and it was László Szíjj in whose interest it was — on the deck of whose luxury yacht Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó had vacationed. Péter Magyar touched on the fact that the Ministry of National Economy and Energy filed a criminal complaint at the end of July regarding the state financing of Duna Aszfalt’s investment in Congo and Zambia. Two state-owned banks, Exim and MFB, subscribed to 126 billion forints’ worth of bonds under the Orbán government in connection with the extremely high-risk African deal — and did so despite the Hungarian state having provided guarantees for approximately 80 percent of the financing, he pointed out. He added that all of this occurred in relation to an investment tied to countries classified in the highest country-risk category. The prime minister reported that Duna Aszfalt, just a few weeks after the criminal complaint was filed, announced it would redeem these bonds at face value, including accrued interest. This could eliminate the Hungarian state’s financial exposure of more than 100 billion forints, the prime minister stressed. Péter Magyar also touched on the fact that, beyond this, public funds in the order of 100 billion forints had already been recovered and safeguarded — for example, in connection with the operation of the M6 motorway and the construction of the Danube bridge at Mohács. He added that the government has filed criminal complaints in more than 20 serious cases relating to the previous administration’s use of public funds, that audits are ongoing across ministries, and that the total amount implicated in the complaints exceeds 1,700 billion forints. The Prime Minister announced that criminal complaints had been filed in connection with the procurement of Egyptian railway carriages — involving an unresolved sum of 640 billion forints — as well as regarding the Hungarian state loan of 360 billion forints granted to North Macedonia, the Gondosóra programme, the KRÉTA, Neptun and Poseidon systems, ambulance procurements, and, among other matters, government communication and support contracts worth tens of billions of forints. He indicated that the National Bureau of Investigation has already ordered investigations in several cases. He announced that on Tuesday the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had filed a criminal complaint in connection with the 300-billion-forint “ventilator scam” linked to “the circle of Péter Szijjártó.” Péter Magyar stated that asset recovery does not stop at criminal complaints: they will separate from the state “the parasitic companies clinging to it,” whose entrenchment has burdened the state — and with it the Hungarian people — by hundreds of billions of forints. For this reason, they decided to withdraw from the Orbán government’s Zugló office deal and not to move into the headquarters linked to “the Tiborcz business circle,” and for this reason they ordered a comprehensive review of the entire relationship between the Hungarian state and the 4iG group of companies. The company’s state contracts, loans and guarantees will also be examined, as will the transactions surrounding Antenna Hungária, the Vodafone acquisition, and the transfers of defence industry ownership, he added. All major corporate and concession-related ties will also come under scrutiny — ties through which “the oligarchs and janissaries of the NER” repeatedly benefited, while the Hungarian state and the Hungarian people suffered. What was outsourced or stolen will be reclaimed, and the state will exit contracts that were unfavourably imposed upon it, said Péter Magyar. He indicated that on Monday the government also discussed the assets and responsibilities of those public-interest asset management foundations (kekva) that do not carry out higher education activities. The Orbán government transferred a total of more than 3,000 billion forints’ worth of public assets into the kekva system — assets created by the work of generations and which should be serving the Hungarian people, he said. The prime minister stated that a portion of these assets had already been successfully recovered, and that for the non-higher-education foundations, the reversion of state assets and the settling of accounts with the state would be completed by the end of August. According to Péter Magyar, Fidesz is using every means at its disposal to prevent the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office from getting off the ground — but to no avail. They may fight and try to slow the work down, but they already know — just as Orbán’s relatives, business partners, and friends know — that whatever was unlawfully removed from the common assets of the Hungarian people will be reclaimed by the Hungarian state, he added. Péter Magyar sent a message to all those who, over the past decade and a half, “built up fortunes worth hundreds of billions as favourites of the state”: follow the example of Duna Aszfalt. Anyone into whose hands public money ended up in a way it should not have, he said, should return it voluntarily now — because the Hungarian state will recover it through legal means sooner or later. The Prime Minister recalled that one of their most important commitments to the Hungarian people had been to recover the wealth stolen from them — and that this commitment would be fulfilled.
